articles.title: British chess prodigy, 11, becomes youngest woman grandmaster
articles.summary: The 11-year-old has broken another chess record after a remarkable performance representing England.
articles.content:
A British child chess prodigy has become the youngest player in history to earn the woman grandmaster (WGM) title.

Bodhana Sivanandan, 11, from north-west London, secured her third and final WGM norm - a certified title-level performance - while representing England at the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, the International Chess Federation (FIDE) confirmed.

Speaking to FIDE, Sivanandan said she was happy about the achievement but wanted to "keep making history".

It is the latest milestone in a remarkable rise for the schoolgirl, who has already become Britain's youngest women's chess champion and the youngest person to represent England internationally in any sport.

Sivanandan, from Harrow, played all 11 rounds on England's top board - a position assigned to the team's top player - and finished the tournament with eight points.

She had already passed the 2300 rating threshold required for the WGM title before securing her third and final norm.

She told Fide in an interview on Sunday about making history: "I'm happy to do it, but I want to keep going and keep making history as well, instead of just stopping here."

Kateryna Lagno, who has represented both Russia and Ukraine, previously held the age record for the WGM title, having achieved it aged 12. Hou Yifan, from China, also achieved the title at 12 and remains the youngest woman to have earned the higher, open grandmaster (GM) title, which she achieved aged 14.

Woman grandmaster is the highest woman only title a female player can attain and the rank is held for life.

Sivanandan's success in Samarkand also earned her a second International Master (IM) norm, taking her another step towards the higher title.

Players normally need three qualifying norms and a rating of at least 2400 to become an international master. Sivanandan now has two IM norms.

The international master title, open to both sexes, ranks higher than Sivanandan's current accolades - the woman grandmaster and woman international master titles.

Speaking to Fide about her love of the game, she added: "I like travelling and also because I do full-time school as well, it links to loads of school subjects, so it's really useful there as well."

articles.title: Soft productivity is the smarter way to work, and here’s how to start
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s a kind of workday most of us know too well. You’re logged on early, you barely step away for lunch, and by 6 pm you’re not entirely sure what you have to show for it. The calendar was full. The inbox moved. But the work you wanted to […]
The post Soft productivity is the smarter way to work, and here’s how to start first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

There’s a kind of workday most of us know too well. You’re logged on early, you barely step away for lunch, and by 6 pm you’re not entirely sure what you have to show for it. The calendar was full. The inbox moved. But the work you wanted to get done? It’s still sitting there.

If that sounds familiar, you’re not failing at productivity. You’re probably just keeping at a version of it that doesn’t work for you.

What soft productivity means in practice

Soft productivity comes out of the “soft living” movement. The idea is to stop letting a to-do list drive your entire day until time runs out, and instead choose a small number of tasks that matter, then protect the energy you need to do them well. “This approach values sustainable energy and focus over completing an entire to-do list without pausing,” says Alexis Verbin, a licensed clinical social worker (L.C.S.W.) at Wellcore Healing. “Instead, a few meaningful tasks are identified and prioritized, with restorative breaks built into the schedule.”

HJ Cho, L.C.S.W., who specializes in grief and anxiety, thinks about it through the lens of intention: “Soft productivity is anchored in the understanding that intention is what makes productivity sustainable.” Traditional productivity cares about output: how much you finished, how fast, how busy you looked. Soft productivity asks a more useful question: what needs to get done, and what does that work take from you?

Why pushing harder usually backfires

Most people don’t need convincing that burnout is bad. What’s harder to sit with is that the same thinking causing the burnout is making your work worse in real time. “The more we push ourselves without breaks and balance, the less focused, creative, efficient, and accurate we become,” Verbin says.

Hustle culture’s logic is hard to escape even when you’re running on empty. “This stems from the idea that every hour on the calendar must be filled with something productive,” Verbin says. “Rest isn’t allowed until everything is finished. But because a to-do list is never truly complete, the daily rest our minds and bodies require is constantly pushed aside.” It’s a design flaw, not a personal one. The system keeps you moving without letting you recover, and you arrive each day with a little less than you had the day before.

How to bring soft productivity into your day

You don’t have to rethink your whole approach to work. A few small things make a real difference.

Protect your high-energy hours

Most people burn their sharpest hours on low-stakes tasks: clearing the inbox, checking notifications, dealing with whatever came in overnight. Cho says that’s backwards. “Most people default to the smaller tasks first, which means the work that matters gets the least capacity,” she says. Save the admin for when your focus has already dipped. Keep your best hours for the work that needs them.

Name your “good enough” standard before you start

Perfectionism isn’t inherently the problem. Applying it to everything equally is. “Perfectionism can produce high-quality work, but it can also turn a 45-minute task into a four-hour project,” Verbin says. Before you start anything, decide what done looks like. A polished client report might need two careful read-throughs; an internal message needs one pass. “Name the bar before you start, and stop when you reach the predefined standard of ‘good enough,'” Verbin says.

Put your breaks in the calendar

If you’re not scheduling breaks, you’re probably skipping them. “Before you know it, it’s 4:59 pm, and you haven’t taken a break yet,” Verbin says. She recommends treating breaks like meetings: a real slot on the calendar, not something you squeeze in if there’s time. The activity doesn’t need to be elaborate: a short walk, a cup of tea, five minutes of fresh air. Your brain comes back differently when it’s had a real rest.

Visibility and productivity are not the same thing

Soft productivity asks you to stop measuring your output by how visible your effort looks. Staying late, staying logged on, appearing available at all hours: none of that is the same as doing good work. “Visibility and productivity are not synonymous,” Cho says. People come to their days with different energy and different bandwidth. Releasing the pressure to perform productivity is, for most people, what finally clears the way for doing it.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.

articles.title: My hometown shows that high streets have to change or die
articles.summary: Aberdeen is launching an ambitious bid to revive its struggling centre. Could it offer lessons for other high streets?
articles.content:
The empty building that used to be the home of Marks & Spencer in Aberdeen is one of the first things you see when you arrive off the train and come into the city centre. The sign has gone, though the shape of the lettering can still be made out; the windows are blacked out and the doors boarded up.

This is my hometown. As a teenager, I spent hours on Union Street, its main thoroughfare, nicknamed the Granite Mile after the local silver-grey stone. It was the place to try on all the latest fashions from the likes of Clockhouse and Chelsea Girl.

The street used to be packed with shoppers from across the north-east of Scotland.

Now, it's pockmarked with empty shops.

"I come to Union Street to take a bus somewhere else... there's nothing to shop for now… it's horrendous," complains Marie Sim, a lifelong Aberdeen resident.

It's a similar story across the country: High Streets, once bursting with shops, hit first by the rise of out-of-town retail centres and then by online commerce.

But Aberdeen is in the thick of an ambitious turnaround plan. The port city has essentially declared war on its empty shop problem, taking an unusually hands-on approach to filling vacant units and bringing long-neglected upper floors of buildings into use.

articles.title: These medieval graves looked like family burials. DNA told a different story
articles.summary: Ancient DNA shows that adults and children buried together in medieval Sweden were often not members of the same immediate family, suggesting that burial choices reflected more than biological kinship. The research also revealed early gender-based burial customs and uncovered the remarkable story of a young woman who may have completed a pilgrimage across Europe.
articles.content:
When archaeologists uncover adults and children buried together in medieval graves, a natural assumption is that they belonged to the same family. New research from Stockholm University, published in Science Advances, suggests that was often not the case.

Scientists analyzed DNA from 142 people who lived during the late Viking Age and Middle Ages. The group included more than 60 children and adolescents recovered from multiple graves at Sigtuna, near Stockholm, Västerhus in Jämtland, and Fjälkinge in Skåne.

Shared Graves Were Often Not Family Graves

The genetic evidence revealed that close biological relatives were surprisingly uncommon among people placed in the same grave. This was true even in cemeteries where researchers found many biological family connections among the wider population.

"We often assume that adults and children sharing a grave were parents and children or other close family members. In most cases, that was not what we found," says Maja Krzewińska, Centre for Palaeogenetics, Department of Archaeology and Classical Studies, Stockholm University, lead author of the study.

The findings indicate that decisions about who was buried together were often shaped by more than close biological relationships. Social, religious, or other community factors may also have played an important role.

"Archaeologists have debated the relationships between people buried together in this type of grave for a long time. Ancient DNA has finally given us the tool we have been waiting for to test these interpretations directly," says Anna Kjellström, researcher at the Department of Archaeology and Classical Studies, Stockholm University.

Children Followed Adult Burial Customs

The DNA analysis also provided new clues about childhood in early Christian Scandinavia. Ancient DNA allowed researchers to determine the biological sex of children whose remains were too young for sex to be identified reliably from their bones.

The burial patterns showed that boys and girls often followed the same cemetery customs as adult men and women. At Västerhus, for instance, men and women were generally buried on different sides of the churchyard. Boys and girls were placed according to that same pattern.

The researchers say this suggests that gender identity was recognized from an early stage of life and was reflected in burial practices.

"The children were not treated as a separate category. In death, they appear to have been treated according to the same social and religious principles as adult men and women," says Anders Götherström, Professor of Molecular Archaeology, Centre for Palaeogenetics, Department of Archaeology and Classical Studies, Stockholm University.

DNA Reconstructs One Medieval Family

Among the people buried at Västerhus, researchers also reconstructed the story of an especially notable family.

A woman identified as Lady 56 was genetically connected to several other people buried in the churchyard. DNA linked her to her parents, her brother, and two daughters. But evidence from her grave suggests that her life may have stretched far beyond the local community in Jämtland.

Lady 56 was buried with a scallop shell, an unusual object to find in a medieval Scandinavian grave. The shell was also a widely recognized symbol associated with pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela in northwestern Spain.

Its presence suggests that Lady 56 may have completed one of medieval Europe's most famous pilgrimages, traveling thousands of kilometers across the continent to the western edge of Christian Europe before eventually returning home.

Lady 56 died before the age of 30. Her parents, brother, and daughters were also buried in different parts of the same cemetery in Jämtland.

Ancient DNA Opens a Window Into Medieval Society

Together, the findings show how archaeogenetics can reveal far more than biological family relationships. By combining ancient DNA with archaeological evidence, researchers can begin to reconstruct how medieval communities were organized, how children were treated, how religious customs shaped burial practices, and how people related to one another in both life and death.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery using ancient DNA to reveal new insights into medieval burial customs, social organization, and gender identity, providing meaningful understanding of historical human societies beyond biological kinship. The research has broad cultural and historical significance, offering a tangible benefit to society's knowledge of the past.

They discovered that adults and children buried together were usually not close biological relatives. The study also showed that burial customs followed gender patterns even among children, and revealed the story of a young woman who may have traveled on a long pilgrimage across Europe.

Elle révèle aussi que les garçons et les filles étaient enterrés selon les coutumes liées au genre des adultes, ce qui signifie que l'identité de genre était reconnue tôt dans la vie. **Contexto** – Los arqueólogos suelen encontrar adultos y niños enterrados juntos en tumbas medievales y suponen que eran familiares cercanos. Un nuevo estudio que usa ADN antiguo cuestiona esta idea al examinar tumbas de Suecia medieval.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de Estocolmo analizaron ADN de 142 personas enterradas durante la Edad Vikinga tardía y la Edad Media en tres sitios suecos. Descubrieron que los adultos y niños enterrados juntos generalmente no eran parientes biológicos cercanos. El estudio también mostró que las costumbres de entierro seguían patrones de género incluso en los niños y reveló la historia de una joven que pudo haber realizado una peregrinación larga por Europa.

**Impacto** – Esta investigación es importante porque muestra que las decisiones sobre las tumbas estaban influenciadas por más que solo la familia. Las conexiones sociales, religiosas y comunitarias tuvieron un papel importante. También revela que niños y niñas eran enterrados siguiendo costumbres de género adulto, lo que indica que la identidad de género se reconocía desde temprano. El hallazgo de una mujer con una concha de peregrino sugiere que las personas medievales podían viajar lejos y tenían vidas complejas.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos continuarán usando ADN antiguo para estudiar más tumbas y aprender cómo vivían y se organizaban las comunidades medievales. Este método ayuda a descubrir detalles sobre relaciones sociales, creencias y costumbres que los huesos solos no pueden contar.
